home.title: Every release gets a flight plan
home.tagline: Previews, canaries and rollbacks for teams without an ops team
home.intro: A release should feel like a launch sequence, not a leap of faith. Lodestar puts a flight plan around every deploy — previews before merge, canaries before full traffic, rollback before anyone finishes typing a status update.

pricing.includes: Unlimited projects · canary releases · release checks · 30-day flight recorder
SSO · audit exports · private regions · dedicated support channel

features.title: Preview environments
features.summary: Every pull request becomes a running copy of your app, on its own URL.
features.body:
Open a pull request and Lodestar builds the branch, provisions a database seeded from your fixtures, and posts the URL back to the PR. Reviewers click a link instead of checking out the branch.

## What's in a preview

- The app, built from the branch head
- A disposable database with your seed data
- Environment variables scoped to previews — never production secrets
- A comment on the PR that updates with every push

Previews expire when the PR closes, so nothing is left running over the weekend.

features.title: Canary releases
features.summary: New versions reach a slice of traffic first, and only spread when the checks pass.
features.body:
A merge doesn't have to mean an all-at-once cutover. Lodestar routes a slice of production traffic to the new version and holds it there while your release checks run against real requests.

## The staged path

1. Deploy the new version alongside the old one
2. Shift an initial slice of traffic — you pick the size
3. Run your checks against the canary's live metrics
4. Widen in steps, or pull back automatically on a failed check

The rollout plan lives in `lodestar.yml`, next to the code it ships:

```yaml
rollout:
  steps: [5%, 25%, 100%]
  hold: 10m
  checks: [error-rate, p95-latency]
```

features.title: Instant rollback
features.summary: Any past release can be back in production before the incident channel fills up.
features.body:
Every release is immutable: the build, the config and the migrations that shipped with it are kept together. Rolling back means routing traffic to a version that already exists — not rebuilding an old commit under pressure.

Rollbacks are one action from the dashboard, the CLI or a failed release check. If a canary check fails, the pullback happens on its own and the release is marked with the check that tripped it.

> The fastest incident is the one that ends before anyone writes a status update.

features.title: Release checks
features.summary: Declare what healthy means, and no release advances without proving it.
features.body:
A release check is a rule the rollout must satisfy before it widens: error rate under a threshold, latency inside a budget, a smoke test returning green, a queue staying drained.

## Checks you can declare

- **Metric gates** — error rate, latency percentiles, saturation
- **Synthetic probes** — HTTP checks against the canary from multiple regions
- **Custom hooks** — any script that exits zero, run against the new version

Checks run at every step of a staged rollout. A failure stops the spread and, if you've enabled it, pulls the release back without waiting for a human.

features.title: Sealed configuration
features.summary: Secrets are encrypted per environment and versioned with the release that used them.
features.body:
Configuration in Lodestar is sealed to an environment: production secrets can't leak into previews, and a preview's throwaway credentials never reach production.

Every release records the configuration version it shipped with. When you roll back, the config rolls back with it — no hunting for the value a variable had last Tuesday.

## How teams use it

- Rotate a key, and the change lands as a config release with its own diff
- Grant read access by environment, so contractors see staging and nothing else
- Pull values locally with `lodestar env pull` for development against real shapes

features.title: Flight recorder
features.summary: A single timeline of every deploy, check, config change and rollback.
features.body:
When something breaks, the first question is always the same: what changed? The flight recorder answers it in one place — every deploy, traffic shift, check result, config change and rollback, in order, with who triggered it and why.

Each entry links back to the pull request and the release it belongs to, so the path from "alert" to "the commit that did it" is a scroll, not an investigation.

Timelines can be exported for audits, and kept as long as your plan allows.

integrations.name: GitHub
integrations.summary: Previews on every pull request, checks reported back as commit statuses.
integrations.body:
Connect a repository and Lodestar listens for pull requests: every PR gets a preview environment, every push updates it, and the preview URL lands in the PR conversation.

Release checks report back as commit statuses, so a rollout that failed its canary is visible right where the code was merged.

integrations.name: GitLab
integrations.summary: Merge request previews and pipeline-triggered rollouts.
integrations.body: The GitLab integration mirrors the GitHub one: previews per merge request, statuses on the MR, and rollouts that can be triggered from the tail of an existing pipeline instead of replacing it.

integrations.name: Slack
integrations.summary: Rollouts, check failures and pullbacks, narrated in your channel.
integrations.body:
Point Lodestar at a channel and it narrates the release: rollout started, canary holding, check failed, traffic pulled back. Each message links to the flight recorder entry.

Quiet by default — one thread per release, not one message per event.

integrations.name: Datadog
integrations.summary: Use your existing monitors as release checks.
integrations.body:
Any Datadog monitor can gate a rollout. Pick monitors per project or per rollout step; a monitor in alert state stops the spread, and the flight recorder records which one tripped.

No duplicate thresholds — the numbers your on-call already trusts are the ones your releases answer to.

integrations.name: Grafana
integrations.summary: Release annotations on the dashboards you already watch.
integrations.body: Every deploy, traffic shift and pullback lands as an annotation on the Grafana dashboards you choose. When a graph bends, the vertical line next to it says why.

integrations.name: PagerDuty
integrations.summary: Automatic pullbacks can open, and close, incidents.
integrations.body:
When a canary check fails and Lodestar pulls a release back, it can open a PagerDuty incident with the tripped check attached — and resolve it once traffic is stable on the previous version.

The incident timeline links to the flight recorder, so the postmortem starts half-written.

integrations.name: Terraform
integrations.summary: Manage projects, environments and checks as code.
integrations.body: The Lodestar provider manages projects, environments, sealed variables and release checks from your existing Terraform workspace. Review infrastructure and rollout policy in the same pull request.

integrations.name: Linear
integrations.summary: Releases link back to the issues they shipped.
integrations.body: Lodestar reads issue references from merged pull requests and attaches them to the release. An issue's page shows the release that shipped it; a release's notes list the issues it closed.

customers.name: Ferrostack
customers.summary: “We stopped treating Friday afternoon like a threat.”
customers.body:
Ferrostack runs payment reconciliation for mid-size marketplaces — the kind of workload where a bad deploy doesn't show up as a broken button, it shows up as money in the wrong column.

Before Lodestar, releases were scheduled around the finance calendar and shepherded by two senior engineers. Now every merge rolls out as a canary gated on their own reconciliation-drift monitor.

> The checks are the same ones our on-call watches. The difference is that now a release has to pass them before it's allowed to spread.

Rollouts happen whenever the work is ready — including Friday afternoon.

customers.name: Nordwind Mobility
customers.summary: “Preview environments turned our design reviews from meetings into links.”
customers.body:
Nordwind builds charging-station software for fleet operators across the Nordics. Their product team is spread over four time zones, and their old review flow was a weekly call with screen sharing.

With Lodestar, every pull request carries a seeded preview: reviewers open a running app with realistic fleet data, on their own schedule, and leave comments on the PR.

The weekly call still exists — it's just about decisions now, not demos.

customers.name: Hexlight Studio
customers.summary: “Client sites ship the day they're approved, not the sprint after.”
customers.body:
Hexlight is an eight-person studio shipping product sites and small apps for a rotating cast of clients. No two projects share a stack, and nobody wants to be the person who remembers how project #14 deploys.

Lodestar gives every project the same launch ritual: preview on PR, canary on merge, rollback on the dashboard. Onboarding a freelancer now means sharing a link, not a runbook.

> The deploy story used to be different for every client. Now it's the boring part of the project — which is exactly what a deploy story should be.

customers.name: Cascade Health
customers.summary: “The audit conversation went from a week of screenshots to a CSV export.”
customers.body:
Cascade builds scheduling and intake tools for outpatient clinics, which means every release conversation eventually becomes a compliance conversation.

The flight recorder changed the shape of their audits: every deploy, config change and rollback is already on one timeline, with who and why attached. When the auditor asks what changed in March, the answer is an export, not an archaeology project.

Sealed configuration closed the other gap — contractors work against staging values and have never seen a production secret.

customers.name: Playdeck
customers.summary: “Canaries caught the regression our load tests missed.”
customers.body:
Playdeck makes live-ops tooling for indie game studios. Their traffic is spiky and superstitious: launch nights bring player load no staging environment reproduces honestly.

Their releases now go out as canaries held against p95 latency during real traffic. The rollouts that would have hurt die at the first step, in front of a sliver of players, instead of in front of all of them.

> Load tests tell you how the system behaves under the traffic you imagined. The canary tells you how it behaves under the traffic you actually got.

customers.name: Tidewater Analytics
customers.summary: “Two people run the platform. Lodestar is the third.”
customers.body:
Tidewater ships dashboards for harbour logistics — a two-engineer company with customers in six countries and no appetite for 3am surprises.

They run Lodestar with automatic pullbacks on and let the platform mind the rollouts. When a check fails, traffic is already back on the previous version by the time a human reads the Slack thread.

It's not that incidents stopped. It's that they got small enough to handle after coffee.

changelog.title: Automatic pullbacks on failed checks
changelog.body:
Canary rollouts can now reverse themselves. When a release check fails mid-rollout, Lodestar shifts traffic back to the previous version and records the tripped check in the flight recorder.

- Enable per project or per rollout with `pullback: auto`
- A pullback posts to your incident channel with the check that failed
- Manual confirmation mode is still the default

changelog.title: Synthetic probes from three regions
changelog.body: Release checks can now include HTTP probes that hit your canary from three regions at once. A probe passes only when every region agrees, so a regional network wobble can't wave a bad release through.

changelog.title: Config diffs in the flight recorder
changelog.body: Configuration changes now appear in the flight recorder as diffs — variable names always, values only for teammates with read access to that environment. Rotations stop being invisible events.

changelog.title: Seeded preview databases
changelog.body:
Preview environments can now boot with a database seeded from a fixtures file in your repo. Reviewers land in an app that has data in it, not an empty shell.

```yaml
previews:
  seed: db/fixtures/demo.sql
```

changelog.title: Rollback from the CLI
changelog.body: `lodestar rollback` promotes any previous release from your terminal. Pass a release id, or run it bare to get an interactive picker of recent releases with their check results.

changelog.title: Release notes, drafted from merged PRs
changelog.body: Every release now carries a draft changelog assembled from the pull requests it contains. Edit it, or ship it as-is to the flight recorder and your team channel.
